The details that make an outing possible “Accessible” can mean almost nothing until somebody tells you about the hill, the gravel, the elevator, the lighting, the quiet corner, the restroom and the walk from the car. This is the standard we use when researching calendar events, Favorite Places and practical guides. We look for current official information first, then use public visitor reports as a secondary reality check when they add useful lived detail. We label uncertainty instead of turning it into a promise. What we checkEight questions before “accessible.”Not every venue publishes every answer. An honest “not confirmed” is more useful than a confident guess. Wheelchair + adaptive strollerStep-free entrances, ramps, elevators, doorway routes, seating, transfer points, wheelchair or mobility-device rentals and whether the route actually works beyond the lobby. Terrain + distancePavement, packed gravel, loose gravel, grass, roots, slopes, long walks, mud, snow and places where a wheeled mobility device may need more help than a general accessibility label suggests. Sensory + communicationNoise, lighting, crowd density, smells, startling effects, quiet spaces, sensory kits, visual supports, AAC-friendly participation, flexible movement, re-entry and whether “sensory-friendly” changes the environment or only the schedule. Blind + low-vision accessBraille, large print, tactile or verbal description, audio description, contrast, wayfinding and lighting changes. We avoid assuming that a wheelchair-accessible route is also an accessible visual experience. Deaf + hard-of-hearing accessCaptions, ASL interpretation, assistive-listening systems, visual announcements, hearing loops/headsets and how far in advance an accommodation must be requested. Restrooms + practical careAccessible and family restrooms, changing tables, and an adult-size or height-adjustable changing table only when a venue specifically publishes that information. We never imply that a particular family uses a facility simply because we report that it exists. Parking + arrivalAccessible spaces, drop-off, distance to the entrance, the best door to use, city parking realities, whether a shuttle runs and what happens after dark. Weather + escape planOutdoor exposure, snow, ice, rain, heat, muddy paths, low light, indoor backup options, break spaces and how easy it is to shorten the visit or leave. Evidence labels How strong is the information? Organizer-confirmedA current event page, ticket page, venue policy or direct accessibility statement. This is our starting point. Venue access guideA current accessibility, visitor, trail, seating or building guide that adds detail beyond the event listing. Public visitor reportA review or public Q&A can reveal practical realities—steepness, crowd bottlenecks, muddy ground, stroller frustration—but it is anecdotal and dated. We label it as such and do not let it override newer official information. Not confirmedWe looked and did not find a reliable current answer. That is a prompt to contact the venue, not permission to guess. See the method in useThe calendar now carries the field notes.Each dated listing can include mobility, terrain, sensory conditions, vision/hearing supports, restrooms, changing-equipment status, parking, weather, a map and a five-step visual visit card.Open the accessible New England calendar ↗ Editorial rules What we will not do. We do not convert “ADA accessible” into a blanket promise about the whole experience. We do not assume a venue has an adult-size changing table, sensory room, ASL interpreter, elevator or smooth terrain unless we can confirm it. We do not present a visitor review as a verified current venue policy. We date access research because buildings, programs, construction, staffing and weather conditions change. We do not diagnose what a person “should” need. The information is there so each reader can decide what matters for their own visit. The website itself Access should apply here, too. We aim for readable type, strong contrast, keyboard-accessible navigation, useful headings, meaningful link text, alt text for informative images, layouts that work on smaller screens, and controls that do not rely on color alone. Visual planners are editable because one person’s helpful wording or picture can be another person’s clutter. Our tools use visible words alongside icons, large controls, familiar examples, keyboard access and clear optional sections. Preselected settings make it possible to finish without adjusting every detail. Color choices always have written names; color alone does not carry an instruction. Our creative standardBeautiful, useful, respectful.Our default look is preppy New England: Nantucket light, Vermont warmth, recognizable objects and natural materials. Communication pictures keep a clear subject and a familiar word. Decoration belongs around the task, where it can add pleasure without obscuring meaning.We create and publish lawful, family-friendly content. Sexual content, graphic violence, hate imagery, exploitation, harassment and deceptive images of real people have no place here. We respect privacy, consent, intellectual property and the dignity of the people we portray. AI-created illustrations are identified as such and are never presented as family photographs or evidence about a real venue.The picture-card studio currently offers a reviewed starter collection and private, in-tab photo selection. It has no public upload gallery and does not generate new images live. Personal photos are not sent to us or automatically inspected. Use only appropriate pictures you are permitted to use. Any future live image-generation service must include input and output moderation before it is made available. If a page is difficult to use—or a field note is wrong, stale or missing—please contact us with the page and the detail that needs attention.

title: A scoop, a phone, and a choice.
summary: An ordinary ice cream outing at Rancatore’s in Lexington, a real flavor-case photo and a family-made choice board. Practical ideas for families and independent scoop shops.

The choice belongs to the customerA case full of ice cream offers plenty to choose from. The question we brought to Ranc’s was how to put those choices in a form James could consider.We were heading to Rancatore’s in downtown Lexington—Ranc’s, as we call it—and I had my phone with me. James, my 14-year-old son, is autistic and non-speaking. Once we reached the ice cream shop, there was another decision waiting for us: the flavors.Rather than try to recite the entire case out loud, I photographed the actual displays and shared them with AI. title: Tourists in Our Own Backyard
summary: A writer, a professor, and an overdue mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge in Concord. Our photographs and watercolors, local history, a map, and practical access notes.
search: Concord, Massachusetts · Time for two Tourists in Our Own Backyard A mid-fall date at Authors’ Ridge. A writer, a professor, three years living nearby—and a little literary pilgrimage we somehow hadn’t made. Our photographs, watercolors, local history, and the practical details for a visit of your own. October 21, 2026 · An AUsome Life Louisa May Alcott’s resting place, from our own visit to Authors’ Ridge. I’m a writer. Dad is a professor. We’d lived here for three years.And somehow, we had never made the trek to Authors’ Ridge. On paper, we were very well qualified to have done this already. But a funny thing happens when you live near somewhere people travel to see: it becomes the place you can visit any time. And “any time” has a way of slipping behind everything that actually has a date on the calendar. So, for a little while this fall, we became tourists in our own backyard. Our date took us to Authors’ Ridge in Concord’s Sleepy Hollow Cemetery, where Louisa May Alcott, Henry David Thoreau, Nathaniel Hawthorne and Ralph Waldo Emerson are buried. Familiar names, suddenly attached to very small, very human places. About the writers and the cemetery. The things people leave behind Look closely at the photographs. Around Louisa May Alcott’s marker are pencils, pinecones, stones and a pink rose. At Thoreau’s, more pencils lie among the roots and needles, beneath a little stone that simply says Henry. I find the pencils especially moving. Such ordinary things, brought to the graves of people whose words have lasted so long. To me, they look like small thank-yous: your work reached someone. Someone is still reading. Hawthorne’s marker has its own quiet simplicity. A rounded stone, a surname, sunlight and shadow. You can know a name for years and still feel differently about it when you stand in front of it, outdoors, at the scale of a person. Henry: a small marker, tree roots, and the things visitors have left. Hawthorne, in patches of sun and shade. In our photographs, the trees still hold plenty of green. A little gold is beginning to show. The ground has its own autumn palette: brown needles, gray stone, moss, a bright flower. There is enough to look at before you read a single name. Before the graves, there were evening walks One of my favorite pieces of this place’s history is that the writers knew it as a place to walk. The National Park Service records that Emerson, Thoreau, and Nathaniel and Sophia Hawthorne enjoyed evening walks in Sleepy Hollow before it became a cemetery. Before these woods held their graves, they held their evening walks. That makes a date here feel part of a much older habit: going outside together, looking around, letting a familiar landscape give you something to think about. Sleepy Hollow was dedicated on September 29, 1855, with an address by Emerson. Landscape architects Horace William Shaler Cleveland and Robert Morris Copeland planned paths and drives around the natural shape of the land, respecting its trees and plants. The Concord Free Public Library’s dedication exhibit describes that approach—and notes that the place already carried the name Sleepy Hollow before it was a burial ground. It belongs to the nineteenth-century tradition of rural or garden cemeteries, where landscape and remembrance meet. The winding roads and wooded setting are part of the history you have come to see. Read about the landscape. A little more of the neighborhood Concord’s history reaches much further back than the writers. The Concord Museum identifies the area as the original homelands of the Nipmuc, Massachusett and Pawtucket tribal nations, and recognizes Indigenous people’s continuing connection to this land. Nearby, the North Bridge holds another chapter: the battle of April 19, 1775. A visit to Concord can open onto many histories. Authors’ Ridge gave us plenty to notice on its own. Something lovely, close to home A date like this makes room for the people we are as well as the people we look after. I’m still a writer. Dad is still someone who loves ideas. And we are still two people who can go somewhere together and find things worth noticing. I like that the visit didn’t need to be elaborate to be worth remembering. A nearby place, a little curiosity, a few photographs. There is a particular pleasure in finally doing the thing that has been waiting so close to home. Three years was a long time to get around to it. I’m glad we finally went. From the photographsA little autumn sketchbook Three watercolor interpretations of our visit. The photographs above show the actual places; these companion illustrations hold their color and feeling. About our editorial artwork. The practical details left inPlan a visit that works for you Cost: free to visit, according to Visit Concord.Hours: town rules list daily opening at 7 a.m. and closing at dusk or 8 p.m., whichever comes first, weather permitting. In mid-fall, plan around the earlier dusk. Check current town rules and posted gate signs. Mobility, ground surfaces & the approach Authors’ Ridge is a hillside visit. The official tourism listing says the approach includes an incline. Our photographs show exposed roots, bare earth and pine needles around some markers. The town’s cemetery master plan acknowledges accessibility challenges from the hills and limited parking. Parking nearer the ridge may shorten the approach; it does not establish a level or step-free route to every grave. If you use a wheelchair, walker or stroller, or need to limit walking, ask the Cemetery Office about your specific route and parking needs before going: 978-318-3233. After rain, take extra care around wet leaves and roots. Restrooms & a place to regroup Plan a restroom stop in Concord Center. The Concord Visitor Center at 58 Main Street lists public bathrooms, and its access guide identifies accessible restrooms inside. Those two pages currently give different opening hours for the facilities. If access to a particular restroom matters to your visit, call 978-318-3061 to confirm availability. Sensory needs, pacing & family planning The photos here are from our date. They do not establish how this outing would work for another person or at another time. Outdoor space can still include other visitors, vehicles and maintenance sounds. If predictability helps, preview the photographs and town map, choose a short first stop, and keep an easy return to the car in your plan. If visiting with someone who uses AAC or other communication supports, keep their usual communication available and make room for “break,” “leave” and “all done.” For a date that depends on someone else covering care, our caregiver handover guide offers a place to put the essentials. Being a thoughtful visitor Sleepy Hollow is an active cemetery. Give funerals and people visiting loved ones plenty of space. Follow the roads and paths, respect the grave lots, and leave markers and existing objects undisturbed. The town prohibits gravestone rubbing. See the cemetery rules for the full visiting and photography guidance. Keep the rest of the date simple For readers who want a second stop, Concord Bookshop at 65 Main Street continues the literary theme. Main Streets Market & Cafe at 42 Main Street is another nearby option for coffee or a meal. Check each business’s current hours and any access arrangements you need. These are ideas for extending your own outing. Or let the cemetery visit be the whole date. One nearby place, finally seen together, can be plenty. title: Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away.
summary: An autumn wedding in New Haven, old college friends from Bristol and Rome, a little time away, and the grandparents who made it possible.
search: From the autumn camera roll · New Haven, Connecticut Old friends, an autumn wedding & a weekend away. College friends from Bristol and Rome, a wonderful wedding, a downtown hotel, and a little time to ourselves. A November 2018 memory · Shared October 22, 2026 All dressed up for a lovely autumn weekend. I've been loving all the old autumn photos that keep resurfacing on my phone lately. Every few days, another little memory pops up — a place we visited, people we love, or a wonderful weekend I'd nearly forgotten about. And these photographs from November 2018 took me right back to New Haven, Connecticut. We were there to celebrate the wedding of our dear friends Deb and Artur, and it was such a lovely excuse to reconnect with college friends from my years in Bristol, Rhode Island, and Rome, Italy. ❤️ There are some friendships that will always remind you of a particular time in your life — the places you went, the adventures you had, and the person you were back then. Seeing everyone again was such a treat. A sweet New England wedding detail, right down to the date on the maple-leaf bottle. A weekend away takes a village. Of course, leaving James for a weekend is never particularly easy for me. As many parents and caregivers know, even the loveliest getaway comes with a fair amount of planning (and perhaps a little worrying!). Thankfully, James was in wonderful hands with Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve, who love him beyond measure and have always been such an important part of our village. Knowing he was with people who know and adore him made it easier to enjoy a little grown-up time. ❤️ We stayed at the beautiful Omni New Haven Hotel at Yale, right downtown. It was such a treat to enjoy a lovely hotel, explore New Haven in autumn, catch up with old friends, and have a little time away from our everyday routines. And the New Haven pizza? Oh, my goodness. 🍕 That's a whole 'nother delicious story, and one that absolutely deserves its own post! Old friends, dressed for the occasion. A heartfelt family remembrance among the wedding details. Dessert, with a side of disco lighting. There may have been some spectacular fashion choices. And yes, the novelty hats came out. 😂 The people are the best part. Deb and Artur's wedding was beautiful, with heartfelt family tributes, wonderful food, lots of laughter, and some truly spectacular fashion choices once the novelty hats and oversized sunglasses made their appearance. But I think what I loved most was simply being together again. There is something so special about friendships that stretch across years, countries, and completely different chapters of life. The people who knew you when you were young and figuring everything out, and who still feel like old friends no matter how much time has passed. And as much as I love sharing adventures with James, these occasional grown-up getaways are part of our story, too. Being a caregiver is a huge part of my life, but so are the friendships, places, memories, and experiences that have helped make me who I am. One more thing worth rememberingGood people make room for good weekends. This getaway was possible because Mom-Mom and Grandpa Steve could be there for James. That kind of trusted family support matters, and I never take it for granted. Not every family has it; it's one reason I believe time for caregivers, and real support to make it possible, is so important. I'm so glad these photos found their way back onto my phone this autumn. A lovely reminder of a beautiful weekend, two wonderful people, and friendships I'm very grateful to have made along the way. ❤️ Here's to Deb and Artur, old friends, and all the stories that follow us home. 🍁 Explore related topics Places & outings Travel & stays
